abstract: Dr. Bothwell presents a comprehensive lecture on breastfeeding for family-medicine residents, covering counseling techniques, latch mechanics, and evidence-based benefits for both infant and mother. She reviews common barriers, complications such as mastitis and engorgement, and management strategies including positioning, antibiotics, and supportive care. The talk emphasizes the importance of continued breastfeeding support and practical resources for clinicians.
key_points: Breastfeeding reduces infant risk of asthma, obesity, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, ear/respiratory infections, SIDS, and necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants.
Maternal benefits include decreased risk of ovarian, breast, and endometrial cancers, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, plus enhanced postpartum weight loss and lactational amenorrhea.
Human milk provides IgA, lactase, lysozymes, and amino acids that support infant gut health, immunity, and neurobehavioral development.
Analgesic effect of breastfeeding during painful procedures may be mediated by higher cortisol levels, as shown in a 66-infant study.
Only 25.4% of U.S. infants are exclusively breastfed at 6 months; 45% of mothers report early undesired weaning, often due to pain, poor latch, or work-related barriers.
Good latch technique: baby's nose opposite nipple, wide mouth, chin touching breast, more areola visible above upper lip, no pain beyond initial attachment.
Mastitis treatment includes continued breastfeeding, warm compresses, and first-line antibiotics such as cephalexin; bilateral mastitis warrants checking baby's mouth for streptococcal infection.
Breast abscess complicating mastitis is often MRSA and requires surgical drainage.
Low milk supply should be objectively assessed by wet diaper count (≥8/day), weight checks (15-30 g/day gain after day 4, <10% loss at week 1, return to birth weight by 10-14 days).
Supportive resources: lactation consultants, employer pumping accommodations per Oklahoma law (2021), and video tutorials for latch technique.
Engorgement usually occurs postpartum day three to five, later in C-section moms by 24-48 hours due to increased stress.
Risk factors for engorgement include extended labor with IV fluids, baby sleeping through the night, and first-time mothers.
